patient.name: Brenda Whitfield
patient.complaint: Six weeks of painful, stiff shoulders and hips; struggles to get dressed in the morning
background: Retired school secretary in Bexleyheath; lives with her husband
Previous wrist fracture after a fall at 66

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a patient over 50 who has bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, a raised ESR, normal CK and normal power, with polymyositis, hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis as distractors. GCA features (headache, jaw claudication) are the classic follow-on.

points: Brenda, 71, has **6 weeks** of aching shoulders and hips.
Stiff for **over an hour** every morning.
Needs her husband to help her **put on a cardigan**.
Feels feverish, tired and has **lost her appetite**.

steps.lead: Proximal pain and stiffness in **both shoulders and hips**: think PMR, and immediately think of its partner, **giant cell arteritis**.
Brenda is **71**. PMR under 50 is so unusual that a younger patient should make you look for something else.

visual.title: Age and PMR
visual.label: Brenda 71
visual.caption: Being **over 50** is a key diagnostic feature of PMR (and of GCA).

points: Cannot lift her arms above shoulder height **because of pain**.
Formal power testing: **5/5** in all muscle groups.
No headache, jaw pain or visual symptoms.

steps.q: Brenda cannot raise her arms, yet power is 5/5. What does this tell you?
o: Movement is limited by pain, not weakness
She has a rotator cuff tear
steps.r: In PMR, active movement is reduced by **pain and stiffness**, but **formal power is normal**. True weakness points to myositis or a neurological cause.

steps.lead: Brenda fits every line: bilateral girdle stiffness, **morning stiffness over 45 minutes**, constitutional upset, and **normal power**.
Brenda faces two risks: **GCA** (which can blind her) and **osteoporosis** from the steroids she will need, on top of her previous wrist fracture.

steps.title: Suspected PMR: what to check
nodes: Ask about headache, jaw claudication, vision
steps.caption: The last box is the safety step: GCA symptoms change the dose and the urgency.

steps.text: Do not pick **polymyositis** because the muscles hurt. Polymyositis causes **weakness** with a **high CK**; PMR causes **pain and stiffness** with **normal power and normal CK**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (ESR and CRP), 'most likely result' questions where CK is normal, and temporal artery biopsy when GCA features appear.

steps.title: Brenda's bloods
steps.text: **Markedly raised ESR and CRP**, mild anaemia, and a **normal CK and TSH** that exclude myositis and hypothyroidism.

steps.lead: No single test proves PMR: Brenda's diagnosis is **clinical**, backed by her raised **ESR and CRP**.

visual.title: Brenda's ESR
visual.label: Brenda 72
visual.caption: PMR typically gives a **markedly** raised ESR. A normal ESR makes PMR much less likely.

steps.q: Which result would most argue against PMR in Brenda?
steps.r: A **markedly raised CK** means muscle damage: think **polymyositis** or statin myopathy. In PMR the **CK is normal**.

steps.lead: Brenda's work-up adds a **bone profile, protein electrophoresis** (myeloma mimics PMR) and a **DEXA** scan: she is over 65 with a past fragility fracture and starting steroids.
If Brenda's picture were unclear, **ultrasound** would show shoulder bursitis; if she develops GCA symptoms, she needs a **temporal artery biopsy**.

steps.text: Investigation lead-ins: **'initial'** in PMR = **ESR and CRP**. Once headache or jaw claudication appear, the **diagnostic** test is **temporal artery biopsy**, but steroids are never delayed for it.
Do not order a **muscle biopsy** or **EMG** for PMR. They are for myositis; PMR muscle is normal because the inflammation is around the joints.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (oral prednisolone, typically 15 mg daily), bone protection on long-term steroids (calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonate), and GCA features demanding immediate high-dose steroids.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for Brenda?
steps.r: **Low-dose oral prednisolone** (typically 15 mg daily) is first-line. NSAIDs are not enough; methotrexate is only a steroid-sparing add-on.

steps.lead: Brenda starts **oral prednisolone**. A **dramatic improvement within days** supports PMR; no response would make her GP stop and rethink.

visual.title: Brenda's first week on prednisolone
visual.caption: A **rapid, dramatic response** within days is typical of PMR and supports the diagnosis.

steps.title: PMR treatment plan
nodes: Yes → slow taper over 1 to 2 years

steps.lead: Brenda gets **calcium and vitamin D**, and because she is over 65 with a past fracture, an **alendronate** too.
These shape Brenda's plan: a **DEXA-based osteoporosis assessment** on long-term steroids, and BSR guidance on PMR and GCA.

points: Four months later Brenda rings: **new right temple headache**.
This morning her right eye went **blurry** for a few minutes.

o: Continue the current dose and review in a week
Wait for a temporal artery biopsy before treating
steps.r: Headache, jaw claudication and visual symptoms mean **GCA**: **high-dose steroids now** to prevent permanent visual loss. Biopsy follows, never delays treatment.

steps.lead: Brenda's GCA symptoms are an emergency: **immediate high-dose steroids** and same-day specialist review.

steps.text: Never hold steroids in suspected GCA while waiting for a **temporal artery biopsy**. The biopsy stays positive for days after steroids start; the optic nerve does not wait.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why power and CK are normal, why PMR and GCA are linked, why GCA causes sudden visual loss, and why steroids weaken bone.

steps.lead: Brenda's pain comes from **bursitis and tenosynovitis** around the shoulders, not the muscle itself, so her power and CK are normal.
Brenda's later GCA is no coincidence: PMR is thought to be part of the **same vasculitis** spectrum.
Brenda's dramatic week-one response reflects a **corticosteroid-sensitive** inflammatory pathway shared by PMR and GCA.

steps.title: Why GCA blinds
nodes: Blood flow to the optic nerve occluded

steps.lead: Brenda's brief blurring was a warning: the next step can be **anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy** and permanent blindness.

steps.q: Why does Brenda need alendronate while on prednisolone?
o: Steroids block vitamin D absorption completely
Steroids suppress osteoblasts and increase bone resorption
steps.r: Corticosteroids **suppress osteoblast activity** and **increase resorption**. A bisphosphonate blocks osteoclasts to protect bone.

steps.lead: That is why Brenda takes **calcium, vitamin D and a bisphosphonate** for as long as she is on steroids.

visual.title: Brenda's prednisolone taper
visual.caption: A slow taper over 1 to 2 years: months of steroid exposure explain the need for bone protection.

mcq.q: Which age group does polymyalgia rheumatica typically affect?
mcq.r: PMR is typically seen **over 50**; this is a key diagnostic feature.

mcq.q: Which condition is strongly associated with PMR?
mcq.r: **Giant cell arteritis** shares the same inflammatory pathway.

mcq.q: What is found on formal power testing in PMR?
mcq.r: Movement is limited by pain, but **power is normal**.

mcq.q: How long does morning stiffness typically last in PMR?
mcq.r: **Morning stiffness over 45 minutes** in shoulders and hips.

mcq.q: What creatine kinase level is expected in PMR?
mcq.r: **CK is normal**: an important negative that excludes myositis.

mcq.q: Which first-line blood tests support PMR?
mcq.r: **ESR and CRP**, both typically markedly raised.

mcq.q: Which investigation confirms suspected GCA in a patient with PMR?
mcq.r: **Temporal artery biopsy**, done without delaying steroids.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for PMR?
What should you do if PMR does not respond dramatically to steroids?
mcq.r: Failure to respond: **stop steroids and reconsider** an alternative diagnosis.

mcq.q: What causes the pain and stiffness of PMR?
mcq.r: **Periarticular inflammation**, not muscle disease, so CK and power are normal.

prompts.q: What is polymyalgia rheumatica and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age over 50 and the GCA link are the two things every stem leans on.

points.p: Inflammatory disorder causing proximal muscle pain and stiffness
Strongly associated with giant cell arteritis
points.why: Ask about headache, jaw claudication and vision every time.

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation of PMR.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem often hides it in function ('cannot comb her hair', 'needs help dressing').

points.p: Bilateral shoulder pain and stiffness with reduced active movement
points.why: Reduced active movement is due to pain.

prompts.q: Which findings separate PMR from polymyositis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'normal power' and 'normal CK' are the two decisive negatives.

points.p: Normal muscle strength on formal power testing

points.why: Polymyositis gives a markedly raised CK.

points.p: Pain and stiffness rather than weakness

prompts.q: What are the complications of PMR?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one comes from the disease, one from the treatment.

points.why: Can cause anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy and blindness.

prompts.q: Which symptoms in a patient with PMR suggest giant cell arteritis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these turn a GP question into an emergency.

points.why: Risk of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

prompts.q: How is PMR diagnosed and what are the first-line tests?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: there is no single diagnostic test; the 'gold standard' is clinical.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis with raised inflammatory markers
points.why: No biopsy or antibody confirms PMR.

points.p: ESR and CRP, both typically markedly raised
points.why: A normal ESR makes PMR unlikely.
Excludes myeloma and bone disease mimics.

prompts.q: What further tests are used in PMR, and when?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: DEXA for steroid bone risk; temporal artery biopsy only for GCA features.

points.p: DEXA if major osteoporosis risk factors (e.g. over 65 F / 75 M, previous fragility fracture, long-term steroids)
Ultrasound of shoulders/hips if unclear: bursitis and tenosynovitis
Temporal artery biopsy if GCA features

prompts.q: Outline the management of PMR, including bone protection.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the response to steroids is part of the diagnosis.

points.p: Rapid improvement within days supports the diagnosis
No dramatic response: stop steroids and reconsider the diagnosis
Calcium and vitamin D; bisphosphonate (alendronate) if high fracture risk

prompts.q: A patient with PMR develops headache and jaw claudication. What do you do?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: treat first, biopsy second.

points.why: Do not delay treatment for it.

prompts.q: Why are power and CK normal in PMR, and why does it respond so well to steroids?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: periarticular inflammation, not muscle disease.

points.p: Pain from synovitis and periarticular inflammation (bursitis, tenosynovitis)
points.why: Muscle fibres themselves are not damaged.

points.p: So CK and muscle strength are normal
Corticosteroid-sensitive inflammatory pathway shared with GCA
Thought to be a form of vasculitis of the same arteries as GCA

prompts.q: Why can GCA cause sudden blindness, and why do steroids weaken bone?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: mechanism questions often ask for the 'most likely cause' of a complication.

points.p: Granulomatous inflammation occludes arteries supplying the optic nerve
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy: sudden, often irreversible visual loss

glossary.PMR: Polymyalgia rheumatica: inflammatory pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles in people over 50.
glossary.Polymyalgia rheumatica: Inflammatory condition of older adults causing proximal pain and morning stiffness with a raised ESR.
glossary.GCA: Giant cell arteritis: granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium arteries, especially temporal arteries.
glossary.Giant cell arteritis: Granulomatous inflammation of large and medium arteries that can cause sudden blindness.
glossary.Temporal arteritis: Another name for giant cell arteritis affecting the temporal arteries.
glossary.Jaw claudication: Jaw pain on chewing due to reduced blood flow to the jaw muscles; specific for GCA.
glossary.Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy: Infarction of the front of the optic nerve, causing sudden painless visual loss.
glossary.Granulomatous: Inflammation with clusters of macrophages and giant cells.
glossary.Proximal: Nearer the trunk; for muscles, the shoulder and hip girdles.
glossary.Polyarthralgia: Pain in many joints without obvious swelling.
glossary.Myopathy: Disease of the muscle itself, causing true weakness.
glossary.Polymyositis: Inflammatory myopathy with proximal weakness and a markedly raised CK.
glossary.CK: Creatine kinase, an enzyme released from damaged muscle; normal in PMR.
glossary.Creatine kinase: Muscle enzyme that rises when muscle fibres are damaged.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; a non-specific inflammatory marker, typically markedly raised in PMR.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, an acute-phase inflammatory marker made by the liver.
glossary.Bursitis: Inflammation of a bursa, a fluid-filled sac that cushions tendons near joints.
glossary.Tenosynovitis: Inflammation of the sheath around a tendon.
glossary.Synovitis: Inflammation of the synovial lining of a joint.
glossary.Periarticular: Around a joint rather than inside it.
glossary.Protein electrophoresis: Blood test separating proteins; detects the paraprotein of myeloma, a PMR mimic.
glossary.Bone profile: Calcium, phosphate, albumin and ALP blood tests.
glossary.DEXA: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scan measuring bone mineral density.
glossary.Fragility fracture: A fracture from a fall from standing height or less.
glossary.Prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid; first-line for PMR at low dose.
glossary.Corticosteroids: Steroid hormones and drugs that suppress inflammation and the immune response.
glossary.Taper: Gradual dose reduction to avoid relapse and adrenal insufficiency.
glossary.Colecalciferol: Vitamin D3 supplement used for bone protection.
glossary.Bisphosphonate: Drug that inhibits osteoclasts to reduce bone resorption, e.g. alendronate.
glossary.Alendronate: Weekly oral bisphosphonate taken upright on an empty stomach.
glossary.Osteoclast: Bone-resorbing cell; the target of bisphosphonates.
glossary.Osteoporosis: Low bone mass and weak bone structure raising fracture risk.
glossary.Temporal artery biopsy: Removal of a segment of temporal artery to confirm giant cell arteritis.
glossary.BSR: British Society for Rheumatology, which publishes PMR and GCA guidance.
glossary.Methylprednisolone: Corticosteroid given intravenously at high dose, e.g. for GCA with visual loss.

technique.stem: A 69 year old woman has a 2 month history of pain and stiffness in both shoulders and hips. She is stiff for 90 minutes each morning and needs help to get out of the bath. She feels tired and has lost weight. Muscle power is 5/5 throughout. There is no joint swelling.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis of proximal pain in an older woman: weakness or stiffness?
Over 50, girdle stiffness over 45 min, normal power; ESR high and CK normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Polymyalgia rheumatica.**

elim: GCA needs headache, jaw claudication or visual symptoms; none are given.
Hypothyroidism gives a normal ESR and often a raised CK.
OA causes pain worse with use, brief stiffness and a normal ESR.
Polymyositis causes weakness with a markedly raised CK.

steps.x: **D. Polymyalgia rheumatica.** Over 50 + girdle stiffness + high ESR + normal CK and power.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has 6 weeks of bilateral shoulder pain and morning stiffness lasting an hour. He has difficulty lifting his arms to shave. Power is normal when tested formally. He has no headache or visual symptoms. His GP suspects polymyalgia rheumatica.
technique.q: Which investigation best supports the diagnosis?

steps.x: Which test supports PMR? Remember the diagnosis is clinical.
Classic PMR; no GCA features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised **ESR and CRP** support a clinical diagnosis of PMR.

elim: Anti-CCP is for rheumatoid arthritis.
CK is normal in PMR; it helps exclude myositis but does not support PMR.
Muscle biopsy is for myositis; PMR muscle is normal.
Nerve conduction studies assess neuropathy, and power is normal.

steps.x: **C. ESR and CRP.** PMR = clinical diagnosis + markedly raised inflammatory markers.

technique.stem: A 72 year old woman with suspected polymyalgia rheumatica started oral prednisolone 15 mg daily 10 days ago. Her shoulder and hip stiffness are unchanged and she still needs help to dress. She has no headache, jaw pain or visual symptoms.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue the same dose for another month

steps.x: 'Next step' after a trial of steroids.

clues: started oral prednisolone 15 mg daily 10 days ago
no headache, jaw pain or visual symptoms
steps.x: No response after 10 days, and no GCA features to justify a high dose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: PMR responds **dramatically within days**. No response: **reconsider the diagnosis** (e.g. myeloma, RA, malignancy).

elim: Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing agent for confirmed, relapsing PMR.
Waiting longer ignores that the lack of response is itself a clue.
60 mg is a GCA dose; there are no GCA features.
IV methylprednisolone is for GCA with visual loss.

steps.x: **D. Reconsider the diagnosis.** No dramatic steroid response = probably not PMR.

technique.stem: A 76 year old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica develops a right temporal headache and pain in her jaw when chewing. The next morning she suddenly loses vision in her right eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale, swollen optic disc.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her visual loss?
o: Granulomatous occlusion of arteries supplying the optic nerve

steps.x: A mechanism question: why has she lost vision?

clues: pain in her jaw when chewing
steps.x: PMR plus GCA features, then sudden monocular loss with a pale swollen disc.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: GCA inflames the arteries supplying the optic nerve: **anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy**.

elim: Retinal vein occlusion gives a 'stormy sunset' of haemorrhages, not a pale disc.
Raised ICP causes bilateral papilloedema without sudden monocular loss.
Detachment gives flashes, floaters and a curtain; the disc is normal.
Vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundal view.

steps.x: **B. Granulomatous occlusion of arteries supplying the optic nerve.** Hence immediate high-dose steroids.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has 5 weeks of pain and stiffness in her shoulders and thighs. She is stiff for over an hour after waking and cannot lift her arms to brush her hair. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. Muscle power is normal on formal testing.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Over 50, girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness, raised ESR/CRP, normal CK and normal power: PMR. Polymyositis needs weakness and a high CK.

steps.x: Diagnosis: proximal pain in an older woman.

clues: stiff for over an hour after waking
steps.x: Plus ESR 68, CRP 41, normal CK and TSH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Polymyalgia rheumatica.**

elim: Fibromyalgia has normal inflammatory markers.
TSH is normal.
OA does not raise ESR/CRP or cause prolonged stiffness.
Polymyositis gives weakness and a high CK; both are normal.

steps.x: **D. Polymyalgia rheumatica.**

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has 2 months of aching and stiffness in both shoulders and hips, worst in the morning for about an hour. He struggles to put on his coat. His ESR is 62 mm/h and his GP suspects polymyalgia rheumatica.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Symmetrical swelling of the small joints of the hands
practice.e: In PMR, active movement is limited by pain but formal power is normal. Heliotrope rash is dermatomyositis; small-joint synovitis is RA.

steps.x: Examination finding in suspected PMR.

clues: struggles to put on his coat
steps.x: Functional difficulty that looks like weakness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pain limits movement, but **power is normal**.

elim: Heliotrope rash is dermatomyositis.
Wasting suggests chronic myopathy or neuropathy.
Reflexes are normal in PMR.
Symmetrical small-joint swelling is rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **B. Normal power on formal testing.** Pain, not weakness.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman has had polymyalgia rheumatica for 6 months, treated with prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. She now has a 4 day history of right-sided headache, tenderness when combing her hair and pain in her jaw on chewing. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 146/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: New headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication with a high ESR in a patient with PMR is giant cell arteritis, the complication PMR is strongly associated with.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a new headache in a PMR patient.

clues: pain in her jaw on chewing
steps.x: Scalp tenderness and **jaw claudication**; ESR 84.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Giant cell arteritis** complicating PMR.

elim: Cluster headache is orbital with tearing, in younger men.
Migraine starts younger and causes no jaw claudication or high ESR.
SAH is sudden thunderclap headache.
Trigeminal neuralgia is brief electric shocks, not claudication.

steps.x: **B. Giant cell arteritis.** Now give high-dose steroids immediately.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has 6 weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. She can get out of a chair but it is painful. Her ESR is 70 mm/h and her GP suspects polymyalgia rheumatica.
practice.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on investigation?
practice.e: CK is not raised in PMR, an important negative that distinguishes it from myositis. CRP is typically raised alongside the ESR.

steps.x: An expected result in PMR.

clues: bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain
steps.x: Classic PMR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Normal CK.**

elim: Anti-Jo-1 is an antisynthetase/myositis antibody.
A raised CK means muscle damage, as in polymyositis.
CRP is typically markedly raised in PMR.
Anti-CCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **C. Normal creatine kinase.**

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman has had polymyalgia rheumatica for 18 months, treated with prednisolone. She did not take any bone protection. She has sudden severe thoracic back pain after lifting a shopping bag. Neurological examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her back pain?
practice.e: Long-term steroids without bone protection cause osteoporosis, and minimal trauma has caused a vertebral fracture. Normal calcium, ALP and electrophoresis argue against the others.

steps.x: Cause of acute back pain in a long-term steroid user.

clues: did not take any bone protection
steps.x: Steroid exposure, no protection, minimal trauma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Steroid-induced osteoporotic vertebral fracture.**

elim: Metastases often raise calcium or ALP.
Electrophoresis shows no paraprotein.
Osteomalacia gives a raised ALP and low calcium/phosphate.
Paget's gives a markedly raised ALP.

steps.x: **E. Steroid-induced osteoporotic vertebral fracture.** Why PMR patients need bone protection.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has 4 weeks of aching in both upper arms and buttocks with morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes. He has lost his appetite and feels feverish. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. He has pain on active shoulder abduction but full passive range and normal power.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bilateral girdle aching, prolonged morning stiffness, systemic upset, high ESR, mild anaemia and normal CK and power in a man over 50: PMR.

steps.x: Diagnosis of bilateral proximal pain with systemic upset.

clues: lost his appetite and feels feverish
full passive range and normal power
steps.x: Girdle stiffness, constitutional upset, ESR 58, normal CK.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Polymyalgia rheumatica.**

elim: Adhesive capsulitis is usually one shoulder with loss of passive movement.
Cuff tears give weakness and normal inflammatory markers.
Myeloma causes bone pain, hypercalcaemia or renal impairment; no girdle stiffness pattern.
RA affects the small joints of the hands and feet with synovitis.

steps.x: **D. Polymyalgia rheumatica.**

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman has 6 weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness, worst for over an hour each morning. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg. Power is normal. She has no headache, jaw pain or visual symptoms.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: First-line tests in suspected PMR are ESR and CRP, which are typically markedly raised. CK is checked to exclude myositis but does not support PMR.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation for suspected PMR.

clues: no headache, jaw pain or visual symptoms
steps.x: Classic PMR, no GCA features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ESR and CRP.**

elim: ANA is for connective tissue disease such as lupus.
CK is expected to be normal; it excludes myositis rather than supporting PMR.
EMG is for myopathy or neuropathy; power is normal.
X-rays show OA, not PMR.

steps.x: **D. ESR and CRP.**

practice.stem: A 75 year old man with polymyalgia rheumatica develops a new left temporal headache and jaw pain on chewing. He has been started on high-dose prednisolone the same day. The left temporal artery is thickened and tender.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Suspected GCA complicating PMR is confirmed by temporal artery biopsy, done after steroids have started. CT head and LP are for other headache causes.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' test for suspected GCA.
GCA features; steroids already started, as they should be.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Temporal artery biopsy.**

elim: Carotid duplex assesses carotid stenosis, not temporal arteritis.
CT head excludes bleeds and masses, not GCA.
Lumbar puncture is for meningitis or SAH.
MRI brain does not confirm GCA.

steps.x: **E. Temporal artery biopsy.** Steroids first, biopsy after.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness for 8 weeks with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. Power is normal. Her ESR is 66 mm/h, CRP 38 mg/L and CK normal. She has no headache, jaw claudication or visual symptoms.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: PMR without GCA features is treated with low-dose oral prednisolone, typically 15 mg daily. 60 mg is a GCA dose.

steps.x: Initial management of PMR.

clues: bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness
no headache, jaw claudication or visual symptoms
steps.x: Uncomplicated PMR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low-dose oral prednisolone (15 mg).**

elim: Hydroxychloroquine is not effective in PMR.
NSAIDs are insufficient alone.
60 mg is for GCA; there are no GCA features.
Physiotherapy helps later but is not first-line.

steps.x: **C. Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily.** Expect a dramatic response within days.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica has been on prednisolone for 3 months and is expected to need it for at least another year. She already takes calcium and vitamin D supplements. She had a wrist fracture after a fall from standing 2 years ago.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management to protect her bones?
practice.e: On long-term steroids with a high fracture risk (over 65, prior fragility fracture), a bisphosphonate such as alendronate is added to calcium and vitamin D.

steps.x: Bone protection on long-term steroids.

clues: already takes calcium and vitamin D
wrist fracture after a fall from standing
steps.x: Over 65, long-term steroids, previous fragility fracture: high risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add a **bisphosphonate: alendronate**.

elim: Calcitonin is not used for osteoporosis prevention now.
Denosumab is an alternative if bisphosphonates are unsuitable.
HRT is not first-line bone protection at 74.
Raloxifene is not first-line and raises VTE risk.

steps.x: **A. Alendronate.** Calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonate on long-term steroids.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica on prednisolone 10 mg daily phones her GP. She has a new right-sided headache, jaw pain when eating and two episodes of blurred vision in her right eye today. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Headache, jaw claudication and visual symptoms mean GCA: give high-dose steroids immediately to prevent blindness. Biopsy must not delay treatment.

steps.x: Initial management: this is an emergency question.

clues: blurred vision in her right eye
steps.x: GCA with visual symptoms: risk of permanent loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Immediate high-dose steroids.**

elim: Aspirin alone does not treat the arteritis.
CT head delays treatment and does not diagnose GCA.
15 mg is a PMR dose; GCA needs high-dose steroids.
Biopsy follows steroids; it must never delay them.

steps.x: **C. High-dose corticosteroids immediately.**

practice.stem: A 69 year old man with polymyalgia rheumatica cannot lift his arms above his head because of shoulder pain, yet power is 5/5 on formal testing. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. Ultrasound of both shoulders shows subdeltoid fluid.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his shoulder pain?
o: Bursitis and tenosynovitis around the joints
practice.e: PMR pain arises from periarticular inflammation (bursitis, tenosynovitis), not muscle disease, so CK and power are normal.

steps.x: Mechanism of pain in PMR.
Normal power, normal CK and subdeltoid bursitis on ultrasound.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Periarticular inflammation: bursitis and tenosynovitis.**

elim: Muscle fibre destruction would raise CK and cause weakness.
Demyelination causes weakness and sensory change.
NMJ antibodies cause fatigable weakness.
Steroid myopathy causes weakness with normal CK, but power is normal.

steps.x: **B. Bursitis and tenosynovitis around the joints.**
